This is a pretty difficult question if you haven't revised the blood group lecture recently, but essentially the answer is O because they are completely incompatible with any other ABO group. This means that if a mother is A and is Rhesus positive, and is carrying an rhesus positive baby, then there is a risk of haemolytic disease of the newborn. This is because the mother can produce anti-D antibodies against the foetus' blood, which can cross the placenta and destroy the foetus' red blood cells. This is only a problem if the mother is rhesus negative. If the mother is rhesus positive, then there is no risk of haemolytic disease of the newborn.  The ABO system is different because the antibodies are naturally produced. For example, a natural BC would be produced by an A mother against an ABO positive foetus. However, these antibodies do not cross the placenta, so there is no problem. This is because the antibodies are IgM antibodies, which are fixated to the Fc receptors on the placenta. However, if the mother is O and is carrying an ABO positive baby, then there is a risk of haemolytic disease of the newborn. This is because the mother can produce IgG antibodies against the foetus' ABO group, which can cross the placenta and destroy the foetus' red blood cells. This is because the IgG antibodies are not fixated to the Fc receptors on the placenta.

The answer is the foramen ovale. This is part of a whole that includes the ductus arteriosus and the fossa ovalis.  The foramen ovale is an opening between the left and right atria that allows blood to move from the right to the left atria to bypass the just formed tricuspid and semilunar valves and the right ventricle and pulmonary artery. It is open during foetal life to allow the majority of oxygenated blood from the placenta to enter the left atrium directly. After birth when the baby takes its first breath, the pressure in the left atrium exceeds that in the right and so the flow of blood from the right to left atria is stopped and in the process the flap of tissue (septum primum) is pushed down to meet the septum secundum and the structure is closed.  However, it does not anatomically close during the first few weeks of life but physiologically it does and so the structure remains patent. Over the next few months the tissue then fuses and the structure is permanently closed, becoming the fossa ovalis.  In some cases the physiological closure is not complete and the structure remains patent, this is known as patent foramen ovale or PFO. This is the condition the little girl in the scenario has.

Cystic Fibrosis is a genetic condition caused by a mutated CFTR protein. CFTR regulates Cl- secretion by acting as a chloride ion channel. In the airways, the movement of Cl- out of cells reduces the osmolarity of the primary effector, H2O. This causes H2O to move out of the plasma and into the airways, keeping them moist and allowing the cilia to function. In cystic fibrosis, the CFTR protein is mutated and does not function as a chloride ion channel. This means that Cl- cannot be secreted out of the cells, and therefore there is no movement of water into the airways. The airways become dry and blocked with mucus.

Calsequestrin is the correct answer. It is found in the ryanodine receptor of the SR and sequesters Ca2+ to prevent spontaneous release. Increased Ca2+ in the cell (ie. via L-type Ca2+ channels during a cardiac action potential) removes this effect and causes calcium-induced-calcium release.  Calbindin is a Ca2+ binding protein that is found in the ER of cells in smooth muscle. It increases the capacity of the ER to store Ca2+ and slows the Ca2+ entry into the cytosol. Calmodulin is a Ca2+ binding protein that is found in the cytosol of cells in smooth muscle. It responds to increased Ca2+ levels by undergoing a conformational change, allowing it to activate various kinases. Phospholamban is a Ca2+ pump inhibitor that regulates the activity of SERCA. It inhibits SERCA in its basal state, but is phosphorylated by protein kinase A (which is activated by cAMP) to remove this inhibition. This allows SERCA to pump Ca2+ back into the SR at a faster rate. This is an important mechanism of calcium-induced-calcium release. SERCA is a Ca2+ pump that pumps Ca2+ from the cytosol into the SR. The PaO2 value tells us that this patient is still hypoxaemic on 40% O2, which is worse than his baseline of >10 on room air. This suggests that the COPD is still causing hypoxaemia, and so we would expect type 2 respiratory failure.  The pH is normal, so we know that there is no mixed picture. The CO2 is low enough to cause acidosis, and the HCO3- is high enough to cause alkalosis. Therefore we can conclude that this is respiratory acidosis compensated by metabolic alkalosis.  This is not unexpected in COPD, as the patient may be vomiting due to increased pressure in the GI tract (as a result of increased intrathoracic pressure), which leads to loss of H+ ions and therefore a rise in HCO3-
